title: Changing personnel and teaching the phrasing
summary: With young jazz sidemen replacing original members, Machito says he teaches them to play tipico with proper attack, dynamics and intonation.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Okay. Macho, in the seventies you are losing or you lost a lot of your men from the original band. You only had John Kins, Pin Madera and a few guys left. You had a lot of turnover in your band, you are getting a
lot of young jazz musicians which really enhanced the sound because they brought new ideas. Did you like it that way or would you've rather hold on to the older men.

Well, I always considered that a change is always, most of the time, for the best; and they was young musicians, very enthusiastic and with good qualifications and not just that it just was good qualifications, they listened to us. They listened to us about what we want and they was flexible enough to play close to what we want, so we was happy, really.

Okay. There are times when you have super sidemen like Chocolaté Armenteros, Jose Chombo Silva, Mario Rivera, Mauricio Smith, and I've heard the band when you didn't have them. They didn't sound as good, but it sounded very good, so you've proven one thing to me, that you always found somebody to fit in with your band. How are you able to do this?

Well, I, is a matter of experience, not that I know all the answers, but I know my music very well and the music is the arrangement that's top-flight because they are made by top-flight arrangers, so when everything is written right and you just read close to what is written, got the sound good.
Yeah, but how do they come out to phrase it the way you want it? Have you told these fellows? Have you instructed them how you want it done?
Oh, definitely. We play and there's a little thing here, there, that they might want to turn their way

and I say: listen, your way is beautiful and is perfect, but you see, this music you just cannot play like Charlie Parker because this is not Afro-Cuban jazz. This is tipico Cuban music. This got to be phrased different. The attack, the dynamics, all the things is completely different than to play jazz. Jazz has its way and this music has its way because this music has its roots and you have to respect the roots of this music like we respect the next one.
There's a phrasing and intonation that gives the Machito sound a unique sound. Do you teach it to these fellows?
All of them, all the new sidemen that come in.
Yes. No, we don't start playing until we get in tune ....
.... it's not that somebody come along from the street and put the mouthpiece and start playing. No, no, no.
